A cache in front of the database (or a read replica) is what relieves read load; for a scoreboard that is read far more often than it changes, caching is the natural fit.

ElastiCache serves the hot, frequently requested score data from memory, which cuts both the delays and the load on RDS without re-platforming the application. RDS Proxy only manages and reuses database connections - useful when an application opens too many connections or needs faster failover, but it adds no read capacity. Migrating to Lambda or to DynamoDB would be a far larger change than the question allows.

gh-31.truth: AWS Config rules are the right answer for continuously checking that resources carry required tags, but AWS Config does not apply tags. It records resource configurations, evaluates them against rules such as the managed required-tags rule, and reports what is non-compliant.
gh-31.answer: A. Use AWS Config rules to define and detect resources that are not properly tagged.
gh-31.why: AWS Config continuously records the configuration of supported resources, including EC2 instances, RDS DB instances and Redshift clusters, and evaluates them against rules. The managed required-tags rule flags any resource missing the tag keys you specify, so the check is set up once and then runs on its own - which is what 'minimize the effort of configuring and operating this check' asks for. Config reports non-compliance; it does not add tags itself. If you also want a tag applied automatically, you attach a remediation action, for example an SSM Automation document, to the rule.

gh-338.truth: An Aurora global database replicates at the storage layer, so the secondary cluster can be created with no DB instances at all - a 'headless' secondary. Replication keeps running and you pay only for replicated storage and cross-Region replication traffic in the second Region, which is cheaper than keeping a DB instance running there.
gh-338.answer: Set up an Aurora global database for the DB cluster and, once setup is complete, remove the DB instance from the secondary Region, leaving a headless secondary cluster.
gh-338.why: Aurora global database replication happens in the shared storage layer, not through a database instance, so data keeps arriving in the secondary Region even when that cluster has no instance running. For a plan that only has to hold a replica of the data, this is the cheapest shape: you pay for replicated storage and cross-Region replication traffic but no idle compute. When you need to recover, you add an instance to the secondary cluster and promote it. Keeping a DB instance running in the secondary Region also works, but it costs more, so it loses on the MOST cost-effectively test.
gh-338.reason: The reviewer is right. The stated answer picks the variant that keeps an instance running in the second Region, which is the more expensive of the two Aurora global database options, and the question is explicitly scored on cost. The item also shipped with no explanation at all.

gh-670.truth: The explanation has the cost comparison backwards, and that makes the stated answer wrong too. Provisioned capacity is billed per capacity unit per hour for all 168 hours of a week whether or not anything is running; on-demand is billed per request with nothing charged while the table is idle. At 4 hours of use a week - about 2.4 percent of the time - on-demand costs a small fraction of provisioned. Reserved capacity is worse still, since it locks in a year or more of hourly charges.
gh-670.answer: A. Choose on-demand capacity mode for the table.
gh-670.why: The table is used for 4 hours a week and sits idle the rest of the time. On-demand mode charges per read and write request and nothing for idle time, so the bill tracks the actual 4 hours of testing. Provisioned mode charges for the capacity units every hour of the month, so roughly 97 percent of what you paid would be for an idle table; on-demand only loses to provisioned once a table is busy something like 15 to 20 percent of the time, far above this workload. Reserved capacity deepens the problem by committing to those hourly charges for a year or more. Knowing the per-second request rate is a distractor - predictable traffic favours provisioned capacity only when the table is busy most of the time.
gh-670.reason: The reviewer is right that the explanation is backwards, and the same error invalidates the stated answer, so both the answer and the explanation are replaced.
